title: Augusta on the Ohio (1797)
summary: Capt. Philip Buckner gave 600 acres to lay out Augusta on the Ohio River in 1797, and the town served as the early county seat of Bracken County.
bodyMarkdown:
Augusta sits on the Kentucky bank of the Ohio River in Bracken County. It grew as a river town, served as the county's first seat, and kept much of its nineteenth-century look. Its founding story begins with a Revolutionary War officer and a large gift of land.

## Philip Buckner's grant

The Kentucky Historical Society's [“Founder of Augusta” marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/founder-of-augusta) says Captain Philip Buckner gave 600 acres to establish Augusta in 1797. Buckner had received land grants, including one in present Bracken County, for service as a commissary officer for Virginia.

The town was named for Augusta County, Virginia. The [Grokipedia entry on Augusta](https://grokipedia.com/page/Augusta,_Kentucky) says the town was incorporated on October 7, 1797, and that the legislature ratified Buckner's land gift.

## Two founding dates

The sources disagree on when Augusta began. Grokipedia and the [Wikipedia article on Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta,_Kentucky) both say Buckner founded it as a trading post in 1786. Grokipedia adds that he explored the area in 1781 and returned in 1796 with about 40 families. The marker gives only the 1797 grant.

Grokipedia also says the town stood on the site of an ancient Native American burial mound. That detail is a reminder that the river bank was a place of Native life long before Buckner's survey.

## A county seat on the river

Bracken County was formed in December 1796, and Augusta soon became its seat. Wikipedia says the seat moved to Oxford, then back to Augusta, before settling in Brooksville. Grokipedia dates the final move to 1839, citing Brooksville's more central location.

Buckner remained a public figure. The marker says he served in Kentucky's second constitutional convention in 1799 and represented Bracken County in the legislature. He lived for many years at his home, "Woodlawn," and died in 1830.

## Ferry, college and war

The Augusta Ferry began in 1798, and Grokipedia counts it among the oldest continuously running ferry services on the Ohio. Augusta College, whose alumni included abolitionist John Gregg Fee, later housed the town's public school.

On September 27, 1862, Confederate cavalry under Colonel Basil W. Duke attacked the town. Home guards resisted, and several buildings burned. Accounts of the numbers differ: Grokipedia cites 450 to 500 raiders against about 150 defenders, while it quotes state marker #501 as giving 350 raiders and 100 Home Guards.

## Kentucky today

Augusta's ferry still links Kentucky Route 8 with Higginsport, Ohio, and there is no bridge at the town. Visitors come for its river front, the Rosemary Clooney House museum and a bourbon distillery that bears Buckner's name.
